title: Neural Crest: One Origin, Many Tissues

scenes.visual: Title: "Neural Crest: One Origin, Many Tissues". Show a gold crest population branching toward peripheral nerves, pigment cells and facial skeleton. Keep these as population-level contributions, without implying that every cell makes every derivative.

scenes.tts: The neural crest supplies nerve cells outside the brain and spinal cord, the glia that wrap nerves, pigment cells, and bone and cartilage of the face. These tissues share an embryonic ancestor. Crest cells form at the edge of the neural plate, then leave and migrate through the embryo. That shared origin explains why gut neurons, hair pigment and hearing can fail together. Where along the body they start helps determine what they eventually become.

scenes.visual: Replace the ganglion-row puzzle with a neural plate whose gold border becomes the crest. Follow descendants toward peripheral neurons, nerve-wrapping glia, melanocytes and facial bone/cartilage. Link gut neurons, hair melanocytes and inner-ear melanocytes to the common crest origin; associate the inner-ear pigment cells with hearing, without showing crest becoming auditory hair cells. End on an axial map.

scenes.tts: In the head, crest makes facial bone and cartilage. Vagal and sacral crest supplies neurons and glia of the gut wall. Trunk crest gives sensory and sympathetic neurons, Schwann cells and melanocytes. In birds and mammals, trunk crest does not normally make skeleton.

scenes.visual: Label head, vagal/sacral and trunk levels on an embryo outline. Branch each level to only the derivatives named in narration. Label Schwann cells as nerve-wrapping glia. Keep the facial skeleton branch attached to head crest, and display the birds-and-mammals qualifier beside the trunk skeleton restriction.

scenes.tts: First, cells need a crest identity. In one proposed network, B M P, Wnt and F G F signals turn on border genes, then crest genes. These control adhesion, movement and later fate. Crest cells loosen their grip on neighbours, lose their top to bottom polarity, break through the basement membrane and crawl away. That change, from a cell in a sheet to a free mesenchymal cell, is an epithelial to mesenchymal transition. E M T.

scenes.visual: Show BMP, Wnt and FGF feeding a simple network: border genes, then crest genes, then adhesion, movement and fate. Transition to a crest cell in an epithelial sheet. Animate loosening contacts, loss of top-to-bottom polarity, passage through basement membrane and departure. Label the change epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT); avoid a universal closed-tube departure sequence.

scenes.tts: Migration depends on the surroundings and on other cells. In the chick trunk, one route runs through the somites, the tissue blocks beside the neural tube. It gives sensory and sympathetic ganglia and adrenal medulla. A later route under the skin gives mostly melanocytes.

scenes.visual: Show a chick trunk cross-section. Label the ventromedial route through the somites and connect it to dorsal root sensory ganglia, sympathetic ganglia and adrenal medulla. Show the later dorsolateral route under the skin ending mostly in melanocytes. Keep this as a route-and-derivative map; remove rostral/caudal exclusion, Eph/ephrin close-ups and ganglion-segmentation claims.

scenes.tts: Crest cells also steer each other. In frog and zebrafish, cells that touch stop moving towards each other and head off in new directions. In frog cranial crest, mutual attraction keeps the group together, while a chemical cue helps guide it. How far this applies to trunk crest in birds and mammals is less clear.

scenes.visual: Show frog and zebrafish crest cells meeting and changing direction, labelled contact inhibition of locomotion. Switch explicitly to frog cranial crest for mutual attraction and chemotaxis toward Sdf1. Keep the group together while it moves toward the cue. Display the limit on extrapolation to bird and mammal trunk crest.

scenes.tts: When crest development fails, several tissues can be affected. In Hirschsprung disease, crest fails to colonise the distal gut. In Waardenburg syndrome, pigment changes and hearing loss can occur together. Some patients have both conditions from a mutation in a single gene. Their different symptoms point back to a shared developmental ancestry.

scenes.visual: Show a gut segment lacking wall neurons for Hirschsprung disease, then pigment changes and hearing loss for Waardenburg syndrome. Join the two in a patient silhouette labelled "some patients: one gene mutation". End on the shared crest origin and its diverse descendants, rather than the old route-exclusion rule.
End card: "Neural Crest: One Origin, Many Tissues". Hold the crest-to-descendants map from the opening.
